topicName: Remote Sensing and Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
description: An introduction to acquiring, storing, analysing and displaying geographic information using remote sensing, GIS and the Global Positioning System, and their growing applications in Tanzania and Africa.

mcq.questionText: What is the meaning of remote sensing?

options.text: The science of collecting information about objects or areas from a distance, usually using sensors on aircraft or satellites
The process of physically visiting a place to measure its features by hand
The act of storing maps in a computer database
Interviewing local residents to gather information about an area

mcq.explanation: Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about the Earth's surface without being in direct physical contact with it, using sensors mounted on platforms such as aircraft or satellites.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a platform used in remote sensing?

options.text: A surveyor's measuring tape
An artificial satellite orbiting the Earth
A printed atlas
A field notebook

mcq.explanation: Platforms are the structures that carry sensors. Common remote sensing platforms include aircraft and artificial satellites, which carry the sensors high above the Earth's surface.

mcq.questionText: An aerial photograph is best described as a photograph taken from which position?

options.text: From the ground looking horizontally
From an aircraft or other platform in the air above the ground
From beneath the ocean surface
From inside a building

mcq.explanation: An aerial photograph is a picture of part of the Earth's surface taken from above by a camera mounted on an aircraft, drone or balloon.

options.text: The science of taking reliable measurements and making maps from photographs, especially aerial photographs
The study of rocks using photographs
The art of colouring satellite images
The measurement of rainfall using gauges

mcq.explanation: Photogrammetry is the science and technology of obtaining accurate measurements and producing maps and three-dimensional models from photographs, particularly aerial photographs.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the five components of a Geographic Information System (GIS)?

options.text: Hardware
Software
Weather
People

mcq.explanation: The five components of a GIS are hardware, software, data, people and procedures (methods). Weather is not a GIS component.

mcq.questionText: In a GIS, which component refers to the trained personnel who design, manage and use the system?

options.text: Hardware
People
Data
Procedures

mcq.explanation: The people (users) component refers to the trained personnel, such as GIS analysts and technicians, who operate the system and apply it to solve problems.

mcq.questionText: Which statement correctly describes raster data in a GIS?

options.text: Data represented as points, lines and polygons
Data represented as a grid of cells or pixels, each holding a value
Data stored only as written text descriptions
Data that cannot be displayed on a map

mcq.explanation: Raster data represent the Earth's surface as a grid of equally sized cells (pixels), each cell carrying a value such as elevation or land cover. Satellite images are a common raster format.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following geographic features would be represented as a line (vector) in a GIS?

options.text: A single water well
A road or a river
A district boundary enclosing an area
A lake covering a wide area

mcq.explanation: In vector data, points show single locations, lines (arcs) show linear features such as roads and rivers, and polygons show areas such as lakes and boundaries.

mcq.questionText: What does the concept of 'layers' mean in a GIS?

options.text: Different sets of geographic data about the same area stored separately and overlaid to make a complete map
The number of computers connected to the system
The thickness of soil shown on a map
The number of people allowed to use the system at once

mcq.explanation: A GIS organises information into layers (themes), such as roads, rivers, soils and settlements, each covering the same area; these can be overlaid to analyse relationships and produce combined maps.

mcq.questionText: What does the abbreviation GPS stand for?

options.text: Geographic Plotting System
Global Positioning System
General Picture Sensor
Ground Photo Survey

mcq.explanation: GPS stands for Global Positioning System, a satellite-based navigation system that allows a receiver to determine its exact position on the Earth's surface.

mcq.questionText: How does a GPS receiver determine its position on the Earth?

options.text: By measuring the temperature of the air around it
By receiving signals from several satellites and calculating distances to them
By taking a photograph of the sky
By connecting to the nearest mobile phone tower only

mcq.explanation: A GPS receiver picks up signals from at least four satellites, measures the time the signals take to arrive, calculates the distance to each satellite, and uses trilateration to fix its latitude, longitude and altitude.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a common application of remote sensing and GIS?

options.text: Cooking food faster
Monitoring deforestation and other land use changes
Composing music
Manufacturing clothes

mcq.explanation: Remote sensing and GIS are widely used to map and monitor land use and land cover changes such as deforestation, urban growth and crop conditions over time.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is an advantage of using remote sensing for geographic data collection?

options.text: It can cover large and inaccessible areas quickly and repeatedly
It always requires no electricity or computers
It gives no information unless people walk on the ground
It can only be used at night

mcq.explanation: A major advantage of remote sensing is its ability to gather data over large, remote or dangerous areas rapidly and repeatedly, which would be difficult or impossible by ground survey alone.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a limitation of remote sensing and GIS technologies?

options.text: They produce maps that can never be updated
They require expensive equipment and trained experts to operate
They can only show very small areas
They cannot store any data

mcq.explanation: Limitations include the high cost of equipment, software and satellite data, plus the need for skilled personnel; cloud cover and data interpretation errors can also reduce accuracy.

mcq.questionText: Which Tanzanian institution is most directly associated with mapping and the production of topographical maps that increasingly use GIS and remote sensing?

options.text: The Surveys and Mapping Division (under the ministry responsible for lands)
The national football association
The central bank
The postal corporation

mcq.explanation: In Tanzania, the Surveys and Mapping Division produces topographical and other official maps, and like many African mapping agencies it now applies GIS and remote sensing in its work.

fib.questionText: The science of collecting information about the Earth's surface from a distance using sensors is called _____.
fib.explanation: Remote sensing acquires data about objects or areas without direct physical contact, using sensors on platforms such as aircraft and satellites.

fib.questionText: A photograph of the Earth's surface taken from an aircraft above the ground is known as an _____ photograph.
fib.explanation: An aerial photograph is taken from above the ground from a platform such as an aircraft, drone or balloon.

fib.questionText: The science of obtaining accurate measurements and maps from photographs is called _____.
fib.explanation: Photogrammetry uses photographs, especially aerial photographs, to make precise measurements, maps and 3D models.

fib.questionText: The abbreviation GIS stands for Geographic _____ System.
fib.explanation: GIS stands for Geographic Information System, a computer system for capturing, storing, analysing and displaying spatial data.

fib.questionText: In GIS, spatial data that is stored as a grid of cells or pixels is called _____ data.
fib.explanation: Raster data represent the surface as a grid of cells, each holding a value; satellite images are a common example.

fib.questionText: In GIS, spatial data represented as points, lines and polygons is called _____ data.
fib.explanation: Vector data use points, lines and polygons to represent discrete features such as wells, roads and boundaries.

fib.questionText: Different sets of geographic data about the same area that are overlaid in a GIS are called _____.
fib.explanation: GIS data are organised into layers (themes) that can be overlaid to analyse relationships and create combined maps.

fib.questionText: A satellite-based navigation system that allows a receiver to find its exact position on Earth is the _____ Positioning System.
fib.explanation: The Global Positioning System (GPS) uses signals from satellites to determine location anywhere on Earth.

fib.questionText: A GPS receiver needs signals from at least _____ satellites to accurately calculate its three-dimensional position.
fib.explanation: Signals from a minimum of four satellites are required to determine latitude, longitude and altitude through trilateration.

fib.questionText: The structures that carry remote sensing sensors, such as aircraft and satellites, are called _____.
fib.explanation: Platforms are the vehicles or structures (aircraft, satellites, drones) on which sensors are mounted to collect remotely sensed data.

tf.questionText: Remote sensing requires direct physical contact with the object being studied.
tf.explanation: Remote sensing collects information from a distance without direct physical contact, using sensors on platforms such as satellites and aircraft.

tf.questionText: Both aircraft and satellites can serve as platforms in remote sensing.
tf.explanation: Aircraft and artificial satellites are the two main platforms used to carry remote sensing sensors above the Earth's surface.

tf.questionText: Photogrammetry is the science of making accurate measurements and maps from photographs.
tf.explanation: Photogrammetry uses photographs, especially aerial ones, to obtain reliable measurements and produce maps and 3D models.

tf.questionText: Hardware, software, data, people and procedures are the five main components of a GIS.
tf.explanation: A complete GIS is made up of hardware, software, data, people (users) and procedures (methods) working together.

tf.questionText: Vector data store information as a grid of equally sized cells or pixels.
tf.explanation: It is raster data that use a grid of cells; vector data use points, lines and polygons.

tf.questionText: In a GIS, layers covering the same area can be overlaid to analyse relationships between features.
tf.explanation: Overlaying layers such as soils, rivers and settlements allows a GIS to reveal spatial relationships and produce combined maps.

tf.questionText: A GPS receiver determines its location by receiving signals from satellites in space.
tf.explanation: GPS works by receiving timed signals from several satellites and calculating distances to fix the receiver's position.

tf.questionText: Remote sensing can only be used to study very small areas that people can easily reach on foot.
tf.explanation: A key strength of remote sensing is covering large and inaccessible areas quickly, which is hard to do on the ground.

tf.questionText: High cost of equipment and the need for trained experts are limitations of remote sensing and GIS.
tf.explanation: Expensive hardware, software and data, together with the requirement for skilled personnel, are real limitations of these technologies.

tf.questionText: Remote sensing and GIS have no useful application in agriculture or disaster monitoring.
tf.explanation: These technologies are widely applied in agriculture (monitoring crops and soils) and in disaster monitoring (floods, droughts, fires), among many other fields.

summary.questionText: Define remote sensing in one sentence.
summary.correctAnswer: Remote sensing is the science of collecting information about objects or areas on the Earth's surface from a distance, using sensors carried on platforms such as aircraft and satellites, without direct physical contact.
summary.explanation: This captures the essential idea that information is gathered from a distance using sensors on platforms.

summary.questionText: Briefly explain the difference between a platform and a sensor in remote sensing.
summary.correctAnswer: A platform is the structure that carries the instrument, such as an aircraft or satellite, while a sensor is the instrument that actually detects and records energy reflected or emitted from the Earth's surface.
summary.explanation: Platforms carry the sensors aloft; sensors do the actual detecting and recording of data.

summary.questionText: What is the difference between an aerial photograph and a satellite image?
summary.correctAnswer: An aerial photograph is taken by a camera mounted on an aircraft or similar platform flying within the atmosphere, while a satellite image is recorded by sensors on a satellite orbiting the Earth in space, usually covering a much larger area.
summary.explanation: The key differences are the platform (aircraft vs satellite), the height, and the area covered.

summary.correctAnswer: Photogrammetry is the science and technology of obtaining accurate measurements, maps and three-dimensional models from photographs, particularly aerial photographs.
summary.explanation: Photogrammetry turns photographs into reliable measurements and maps.

summary.questionText: State the five components of a Geographic Information System (GIS).
summary.correctAnswer: The five components of a GIS are hardware, software, data, people (users) and procedures (methods).
summary.explanation: All five components must work together for a GIS to function effectively.

summary.questionText: Explain the difference between raster data and vector data in a GIS.
summary.correctAnswer: Raster data represent the Earth's surface as a grid of cells or pixels, each holding a value, while vector data represent features as points, lines and polygons; rasters suit continuous data like satellite images and elevation, and vectors suit discrete features like roads and boundaries.
summary.explanation: Raster uses pixels for continuous surfaces; vector uses points, lines and polygons for discrete features.

summary.questionText: Explain what layers are in a GIS and why they are useful.
summary.correctAnswer: Layers are separate sets of geographic data about the same area, such as roads, rivers, soils and settlements, that can be overlaid in a GIS to analyse relationships between features and produce combined thematic maps.
summary.explanation: Layering allows separate themes to be combined and analysed together.

summary.questionText: List four common sources of geographic data used in GIS.
summary.correctAnswer: Common sources of geographic data include satellite images and remote sensing data, aerial photographs, GPS field surveys and ground surveys, and existing maps, statistics and records such as census data.
summary.explanation: Geographic data can come from remote sensing, GPS, field surveys and existing maps or records.

summary.questionText: Briefly explain how the Global Positioning System (GPS) works.
summary.correctAnswer: A GPS receiver picks up timed signals from at least four satellites, measures how long each signal takes to arrive to calculate the distance to each satellite, and then uses trilateration to determine its exact latitude, longitude and altitude on the Earth.
summary.explanation: GPS uses timing of satellite signals and trilateration from at least four satellites to fix a position.

summary.questionText: State three applications of remote sensing and GIS in Tanzania or Africa.
summary.correctAnswer: Remote sensing and GIS are used for mapping and updating maps, monitoring land use changes such as deforestation and urban growth, supporting agriculture and food security, weather forecasting, disaster monitoring of floods and droughts, and planning of towns, roads and conservation areas.
summary.explanation: Any three valid uses such as mapping, land use monitoring, agriculture, weather forecasting, disaster monitoring or urban planning are acceptable.

hoq.questionText: A regional planner in Tanzania wants to identify the best site for a new market that is close to a main road, on flat land, and away from a flood-prone river. Which GIS technique would most directly help make this decision?

options.text: Printing a single paper map and guessing the location
Overlaying layers of roads, slope/elevation and flood zones to find areas that satisfy all conditions
Photographing the area with a camera only
Asking one resident where the market should be built

hoq.explanation: GIS overlay analysis combines several layers (roads, slope, flood risk) so the planner can find locations meeting all criteria at once; this is a core strength of GIS for site selection.

hoq.questionText: After heavy rains, an area is covered by thick cloud for several days, making optical satellite images unusable for assessing flood damage. Which approach would best overcome this specific limitation?

options.text: Wait until the next dry season before doing anything
Use radar (microwave) remote sensing, which can penetrate clouds, together with GIS analysis
Switch off all sensors because nothing can be done
Use a low-resolution hand-drawn sketch of the clouds

hoq.explanation: Optical sensors cannot see through clouds, but radar (microwave) remote sensing can penetrate cloud cover, so it is suitable for monitoring floods during bad weather, with results analysed in a GIS.

hoq.questionText: A field officer records the exact coordinates of dozens of new water wells in a rural district and wants to map them and analyse their spacing relative to villages. Which combination of technologies is most appropriate?

options.text: GPS to capture each well's coordinates, then GIS to map and analyse them against settlement layers
A weather balloon to forecast rainfall over the wells
A camera alone to photograph each well with no location data
A radio to announce the well locations to villagers

hoq.explanation: GPS provides accurate coordinates for each well as point data, and GIS then maps these points and analyses their distribution and spacing relative to village layers, combining the strengths of both technologies.
